points: Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi's famous metaphor in the Kuzari: the Jewish people are grape vines. Being born into the faith is not enough - a vine left unpruned grows wild and does not produce proper fruit. Mitzvos are the pruning that refines us.

Soil shapes the wine: the same vines taste different planted in Baltimore or in Napa Valley. For Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi this shows the importance of Eretz Yisrael - a person can do amazing mitzvos, but doing them in Eretz Yisrael is not the same as doing them anywhere else.
Yechezkel gives the vineyard metaphor a darker turn: the vine is producing no fruit. The fruit is the product of the mitzvos themselves, and the Jewish people of his time were not producing it.

The Abarbanel explains: vine wood is thin, brittle and useless for tools. The Jewish people's impact was never meant to be material strength or physical prowess; it is spiritual. Without the grapes, material success cannot substitute - that is not our role.

When the spiritual role goes unfulfilled, nothing else remains: Hashem says the fruitless vine becomes firewood, meaning destruction. This is why the Jewish people suffer more than others - without fulfilling their spiritual purpose, they have no role left.
